the bulbar urethra in patients with strictures has a decreased collagen type I and increased collagen type III content.
the spongiosal tissues of patients with bulbar strictures have a significantly different extracellular matrix composition and structure compared to normal spongiosal urethral tissue.
the bulbar urethra is a highly specialised organ that is susceptible to a variety of insults that may result in fibrosis and strictures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spongiosal fibroblasts in patients with stricture disease produce an increased amount of collagen, which is characterised by an increased ratio of type III to type I collagen.
bulbar stricture formation is associated with a marked reduction in the collagen type III to collagen type I ratio.

bulbar urethra in patients with urethral stricture is characterised by a significant increase in collagen and elastic fibres and by an increase in the number of fibroblast-like cells, which are responsible for collagen synthesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
spongiofibrosis is a dynamic process and the extracellular matrix of the spongy urethra is a key component of the process of urethral stricture formation and maintenance.
spongiosal fibrosis and stricture formation are not simply due to the deposition of scar tissue.
the bulbar urethra has a unique histological architecture, with a high density of collagen fibres and a low density of elastic fibres, compared to penile and membranous urethra.
